record.title: A paper finds local serving protocols can distort tool-use fidelity scores
record.summary: A September 2026 preprint reports that local serving behavior can be mistaken for model tool-use behavior. In the authors’ Ollama setup, static template flags reject some native tool-call requests before inference; their harness records retry exhaustion as a generic assistant turn, which can make an unrun model appear to have zero tool-call fidelity. Across four serving stacks, request handling differs. Prompt hints improve some accepted models, while forcing a uniform text protocol reduces fidelity for a model with native tool-call support. Turn-pooled and per-seed estimates differ by up to about 55 points when a looping episode dominates a thin sample. These are author-reported results from a small study, not a prevalence estimate or general model comparison.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The authors published a September 22, 2026 preprint that studies serving-layer effects on local tool-call evaluation.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the authors’ Ollama case study, static template flags reject native tool requests for Phi-3 and Gemma-3 before model inference; their harness does not preserve refusal as structured failure metadata, allowing downstream analysis to count the request as a model non-call.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across the reported protocol controls and four-stack probes, fidelity depends on the serving path: adding a text hint helps some accepted models, a uniform text protocol lowers Llama-3.2’s measured fidelity, and turn-pooled versus per-seed estimates differ by up to about 55 percentage points on thin denominators.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The study is a small measurement study and does not establish a general scale law, model-family effect, reasoning/tool-training relationship, or prevalence across local deployments; the authors explicitly disclaim those inferences.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent replay established request rejection, harness error classification and protocol-rate differences.
Prevalence of the reported failure mode across model templates, server versions and evaluation harnesses is unknown.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported protocol confounds recur, request rejection and serving-specific formatting can make model tool-use measurements materially misstate whether inference occurred or whether the model selected a tool. Score 4 reflects a useful measurement-validity result in a small local-stack study, with no evidence of field-wide prevalence.
limitations: All measurements are author-reported; no independent reproduction was performed in this activation.
The study is small and the largest pooled-versus-per-seed gaps arise on thin denominators and looping episodes.
The findings concern protocol fidelity and request handling, not downstream task success or general model capability.
The authors explicitly disclaim scale, model-family and reasoning/tool-training conclusions.
The deployment prevalence of these specific confounds is not established.
brief.summary: A September 2026 preprint reports that local serving behavior can be mistaken for model tool-use behavior. In the authors’ Ollama setup, static template flags reject some native tool-call requests before inference; their harness records retry exhaustion as a generic assistant turn, which can make an unrun model appear to have zero tool-call fidelity. Across four serving stacks, request handling differs. Prompt hints improve some accepted models, while forcing a uniform text protocol reduces fidelity for a model with native tool-call support. Turn-pooled and per-seed estimates differ by up to about 55 points when a looping episode dominates a thin sample. These are author-reported results from a small study, not a prevalence estimate or general model comparison.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report that Phi-3 and Gemma-3 native requests are rejected by an Ollama template gate before inference, and that their harness can record rejection as an ordinary non-call. A native-plus-text-hint control recovers fidelity for several accepted models, whereas a uniform text-tools protocol reduces Llama-3.2 fidelity. Cross-stack probes show differing behavior across Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM and SGLang; pooled and per-seed estimates differ by up to about 55 points.
technical.compute_or_cost: No compute or economic comparison is claimed.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint, protocol description and reported tables are directly inspectable. Numerical results are author-reported and were not independently reproduced in this activation.
technical.mechanism: The serving layer gates tool requests and determines whether a request is rejected, returned as text or emitted through a native tool-call channel. If the harness does not retain transport errors as structured outcomes, a pre-inference rejection can be counted as a model non-call. Prompt channel and per-turn aggregation also affect reported fidelity.
technical.regime: Small local-model tool-call protocol study. Ollama is the primary case study, with probes across llama.cpp, vLLM and SGLang; the paper reports eight seeds for its main protocol rates. The study tests tool-call format fidelity, not end-to-end task success or general agent competence.
technical.reproducibility: The paper describes the protocol and accepted REALM @ EMNLP 2026. This activation inspected the arXiv paper but did not inspect or run an associated harness artifact.
technical.strongest_baseline: Within the paper, matched native, native-plus-text-hint and uniform text-tools conditions on the same models, plus a cross-stack probe. These are author-run protocol controls, not independent replications.

brief.title: A paper finds local serving protocols can distort tool-use fidelity scores
brief.why_it_matters: Tool-use evaluations can conflate model decisions with request acceptance, serialization and harness accounting. Separating transport rejection, non-response, malformed calls and model-selected non-calls could change how local agent results are interpreted. The paper does not show how common these errors are across deployments.
